title: Healthcare systems evolved because care became connected
overview: Trace healthcare systems from isolated departmental tools to connected platforms, distinguish common forms of network access and health-information exchange, and examine how benefits depend on trustworthy information, safeguards, and workable workflows.
objectives: Explain how healthcare systems evolved from isolated departmental systems to connected platforms.
Distinguish the Internet, intranet, extranet, and Health Information Exchange (HIE).
Explain the benefits and risks of electronic health-information exchange and the HIM professional's role in managing them.
Describe principles and responsibilities for ensuring health information is fit for its intended use, trustworthy, and usable in workflow.

concepts.name: Isolated systems
concepts.definition: Early systems that handled a limited task or department and often operated separately from other systems.

concepts.name: Departmental systems
concepts.definition: Systems that automate a department's workflow.

concepts.name: Enterprise systems
concepts.definition: Systems that share information across an organization.

concepts.name: Connected systems
concepts.definition: Systems that exchange information across organizational boundaries with authorized partners.

concepts.name: Internet
concepts.definition: A public worldwide network through which people with authorization and an internet connection can access public websites or online services.

concepts.name: Intranet
concepts.definition: A private network used inside one organization, accessible only to authorized employees.

concepts.name: Extranet
concepts.definition: A private system that gives selected external partners controlled access.

concepts.name: Health Information Exchange (HIE)
concepts.definition: The organized electronic sharing of patient health information between different healthcare organizations.

concepts.name: Connectivity management
concepts.definition: Managing connected information so it belongs to the correct patient, is accurate and complete, is protected from unauthorized access, and appears at the right time in workflow.

concepts.name: Benefits of health-information exchange
concepts.definition: Faster access to records, fewer repeated tests, and coordinated care through providers working with shared accurate information.

concepts.name: Risks of electronic health-information exchange
concepts.definition: Wrong-patient matching, unauthorized access, and incomplete exchange.

concepts.name: Quality, safety, and governance principles
concepts.definition: Principles covering purpose and fit; data and meaning; access and trust; and workflow and adoption, with controls such as scope and workflow fit, definitions and validation, policy and role-based access, and user testing and training.

concepts.name: HIM responsibilities in connected health-information work
concepts.definition: Explain system purpose; protect meaning and quality; protect trust; and improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

sections.body: Early healthcare systems often handled one limited task or department, such as billing, payroll, laboratory reporting, or pharmacy records, and operated separately. The Week 2 framework describes a progression: isolated systems involve separate records and duplicate work; departmental systems automate a department's workflow; enterprise systems share information across an organization; and connected systems allow authorized partners to exchange information across organizational boundaries. Modern platforms may bring together clinical information, financial activity, operational work, and consumer-facing services. This progression describes increasing connection; it does not mean that connection by itself guarantees useful or safe information.
sections.title: From isolated tools to connected systems

sections.body: The Internet is a public worldwide network used to access public websites or online services. An intranet is private to one organization and available only to authorized employees. An extranet is a private system that gives selected external partners controlled access. A Health Information Exchange (HIE), by contrast, is organized electronic sharing of patient health information between different healthcare organizations. The practical distinction is both who is connecting and what the connection is for: an extranet describes controlled partner access to a system, while an HIE is specifically for exchanging health information between organizations.
sections.title: Network access and health-information exchange are not interchangeable

sections.body: Information exchange can support faster access to records, fewer repeated tests, and coordinated care when providers work from shared, accurate information. These benefits depend on the quality and handling of the exchange. Information must be linked to the correct patient, accurate and complete, protected from unauthorized access, and visible at the right time in the healthcare workflow. For example, a laboratory result is useful only when it is associated with the correct patient, accurate, secure, and available to the clinician when needed. A patient moving from a primary-care clinic to a hospital illustrates how authorized exchange of relevant history, medications, results, and referrals can support continuity of care when identity, shared meaning, privacy, and data quality are controlled.
sections.title: Why connectivity must be managed

sections.body: Three risks require attention. Wrong-patient matching attaches information to the wrong person, potentially leading to unsafe decisions. Unauthorized access occurs when someone views, uses, or shares health information without permission. Incomplete exchange leaves information missing, delayed, or untransferred, creating an incomplete picture of the patient. HIM responses include controls such as patient identifiers, access permissions, verification procedures, and release rules; monitoring through access-log review and exchange audits; staff education about identification, privacy, security, documentation, and sharing procedures; and correction of inaccurate or mismatched records and missing information, together with incident reporting or investigation.
sections.title: Risks and the HIM response

sections.body: Reliable information depends on four linked principles. Purpose and fit asks whether the system supports intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; scope, workflow fit, and measurable objectives help address this. Data and meaning concerns whether information is complete, valid, consistent, timely, and understood; definitions, metadata, validation, and mapping support this work. Access and trust concerns privacy, security, integrity, and auditability; policies, role-based access, authentication, and logs are identified controls. Workflow and adoption concerns whether people can use information safely and effectively; user testing, training, monitoring, and improvement support use in practice. HIM professionals connect these principles to information work by explaining system purpose, protecting meaning and quality, protecting trust, and improving workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.

activities.title: Check whether an exchange is ready to help
activities.prompt: Hypothetical situation: A clinician can view a laboratory result received from another organization, but the result may be linked to the wrong patient and is not visible within the clinician's workflow when needed. Which response best reflects the requirements for useful connectivity?
activities.debrief: Connectivity alone is not enough. Information must belong to the correct patient, be accurate and complete, be protected from unauthorized access, and appear at the right time in workflow.
options: Treat connection as sufficient because the result is available somewhere in the system.
Verify patient identity and information quality, protect access, and make the result available at the appropriate point in workflow.
Focus only on giving more external partners access to the system.
Remove the result from the exchange without checking its identity or quality.

pairs.right: Use patient identifiers and verification procedures; correct inaccurate or mismatched records.
Use access permissions and release rules; review logs and audit exchanges.
Complete missing information and report or investigate incidents.
